title: Skeletal muscle contraction
blurb: Order the events from nerve signal to power stroke, explain the roles of calcium and ATP, and match energy systems and contraction types to real activity.
question: After death, muscles lock rigid even though no nerve signals arrive. Which molecule has run out, and which step of the cross-bridge cycle can no longer happen?

teach.h: Filaments slide; they do not shrink
teach.body: Formally, the sliding filament theory states that a muscle fiber shortens when myosin heads bind actin and pull the thin actin filaments toward the center of each sarcomere. In plain English: the filaments themselves keep their length; they slide past each other, overlapping more, so every sarcomere gets shorter and so does the whole muscle. Calcium switches the process on, and ATP powers it and lets it reset.

teach.caption: Fiber vocabulary: sarcolemma = cell membrane; sarcoplasm = cytoplasm; sarcoplasmic reticulum (SR) stores Ca²⁺; T-tubules carry the impulse inward.

steps.label: ACh released
steps.sub: At the neuromuscular junction; binds sarcolemma receptors

steps.label: Action potential
steps.sub: Spreads along sarcolemma and down T-tubules

steps.label: Ca²⁺ binds troponin
steps.sub: Tropomyosin moves off actin's binding sites

steps.label: Power stroke
steps.sub: Myosin heads bind actin (cross-bridges) and pull

steps.label: Relaxation
steps.sub: ACh broken down; Ca²⁺ pumped back into SR

teach.caption: Acetylcholinesterase breaks down ACh. Pumping Ca²⁺ back into the SR also uses ATP.

teach.h: ATP has two jobs at the cross-bridge
teach.body: First, splitting ATP energizes (cocks) the myosin head so it can bind actin and perform the power stroke. Second, a fresh ATP must bind myosin to RELEASE it from actin. With no ATP, cross-bridges cannot detach, which is why muscles stiffen after death (rigor mortis). Each fiber responds all-or-none; whole-muscle force is graded by recruiting more motor units (one motor neuron plus all the fibers it supplies) and by stimulating them more often (summation, tetanus).

steps.label: Anaerobic glycolysis
steps.sub: Fast; 2 ATP per glucose; lactic acid

teach.caption: Myoglobin stores oxygen inside muscle fibers.
Concentric and eccentric are both isotonic: the muscle changes length.

teach.body: Destiny runs an all-out 400 m. Stored ATP lasts only seconds, then creatine phosphate carries her briefly. For most of the lap her fast-twitch fibers rely on anaerobic glycolysis, which is fast but yields lactic acid, the burn she feels near the finish. Afterward, aerobic respiration in her mitochondria takes over. Holding her finishing pose for a photo, her calves contract isometrically: tension without a change in length.

teach.text: Ca²⁺ binds TROPONIN (not tropomyosin or myosin) and comes from the SARCOPLASMIC RETICULUM (not mitochondria). ATP is needed to RELEASE myosin. The filaments do not shorten and the A band stays constant. Isometric means NO change in length. Lactic acid comes from ANAEROBIC glycolysis.

items: Muscle, fascicle, fiber, myofibril, sarcomere, actin and myosin.
ACh at the NMJ, action potential down T-tubules, Ca²⁺ from SR binds troponin, tropomyosin moves, cross-bridges pull.
ATP energizes the power stroke and releases myosin; no ATP = rigor mortis.
Sarcomere, I band and H zone shorten; A band and filament lengths stay the same.
Energy: stored ATP, creatine phosphate, anaerobic glycolysis (lactic acid), aerobic respiration (most ATP).
Force grows by recruiting motor units; isotonic changes length, isometric does not.

summary: You can now order the events of skeletal muscle contraction from acetylcholine release to relaxation, and explain the roles of calcium, troponin, tropomyosin and ATP. You can also describe what happens inside the sarcomere, match energy systems and fiber types to activities, and classify contractions as isotonic or isometric.

A.q: Calcium ions released inside a skeletal muscle fiber bind to which protein to start contraction?
A.why: Ca²⁺ binds troponin, which shifts tropomyosin off the myosin-binding sites on actin.

whyNot.0: Tropomyosin is moved as a result; calcium does not bind to it directly.
whyNot.1: Myosin binds actin and ATP; it is not the calcium receptor.
whyNot.3: Actin carries the binding sites that tropomyosin covers; calcium binds troponin instead.

A.q: In a resting skeletal muscle fiber, where is the calcium needed for contraction stored?
A.why: The sarcoplasmic reticulum, the fiber's smooth ER, stores Ca²⁺ and releases it when an action potential arrives.

whyNot.0: Mitochondria make ATP; they are not the calcium store for contraction.
whyNot.2: The neuromuscular junction is where ACh is released, outside the fiber's calcium store.
whyNot.3: T-tubules carry the action potential inward to trigger release; they do not store the calcium.

A.q: Which neurotransmitter is released at the neuromuscular junction to trigger skeletal muscle contraction?
A.why: Motor neurons release acetylcholine (ACh), which binds receptors on the sarcolemma.

whyNot.1: Norepinephrine is a sympathetic neurotransmitter, not the one at the neuromuscular junction.
whyNot.2: Dopamine works within the central nervous system; motor neurons release ACh onto muscle.
whyNot.3: Serotonin is a brain neurotransmitter, not the signal motor neurons send to muscle.

B.q: Which change occurs in a sarcomere during contraction?
options: The A band stays the same length
The A band shortens as myosin shortens
The thin and thick filaments both shorten
The H zone widens as the Z discs separate
B.why: The A band equals the length of the myosin filaments, which do not shorten, so it stays constant while the sarcomere shortens.

whyNot.1: Myosin filaments keep their length, so the A band does not shorten.
whyNot.2: Filaments slide past each other; neither actin nor myosin shortens.
whyNot.3: The H zone shortens and the Z discs move closer together.

B.q: Why do muscles become rigid after death (rigor mortis)?
options: Without ATP, myosin cannot bind to actin
Calcium is pumped back into the reticulum
Without ATP, myosin cannot detach from actin
Lactic acid builds up and locks the filaments
B.why: ATP must bind myosin to release it from actin. With no ATP, cross-bridges stay attached and muscles lock.

whyNot.0: Myosin binding actin is not what fails; detaching is the step that needs fresh ATP.
whyNot.1: Pumping calcium back into the SR causes relaxation, not rigidity.
whyNot.3: Lactic acid comes from anaerobic glycolysis and does not lock cross-bridges.

B.q: Holding a plank position without moving is an example of which type of contraction?
B.why: In an isometric contraction the muscle develops tension without changing length.

whyNot.0: A concentric contraction shortens the muscle, as in lifting.
whyNot.1: An eccentric contraction lengthens the muscle under load, as in lowering a weight.
whyNot.3: Isotonic contractions change muscle length; a plank holds it constant.

C.q: Which sequence correctly orders these events in skeletal muscle contraction?
options: ACh released, Ca²⁺ binds troponin, Ca²⁺ released from SR, power stroke
Ca²⁺ released from SR, ACh released, Ca²⁺ binds troponin, power stroke
ACh released, Ca²⁺ released from SR, power stroke, Ca²⁺ binds troponin
ACh released, Ca²⁺ released from SR, Ca²⁺ binds troponin, power stroke
C.why: ACh triggers an action potential, which releases Ca²⁺ from the SR; Ca²⁺ binds troponin, exposing actin, and then the power stroke occurs.

whyNot.0: Calcium must be released from the SR before it can bind troponin.
whyNot.1: ACh release at the neuromuscular junction comes first; it triggers the calcium release.
whyNot.2: The power stroke cannot happen until Ca²⁺ binds troponin and the binding sites are exposed.

C.q: Destiny runs an all-out 400 m and feels a burning in her legs near the finish. Which pathway is the main source of the lactic acid?
C.why: Anaerobic glycolysis supplies ATP quickly without oxygen (2 ATP per glucose) and produces lactic acid.

whyNot.0: Aerobic respiration uses oxygen and does not produce lactic acid.
whyNot.2: Creatine phosphate regenerates ATP for about 10–15 seconds and does not produce lactic acid.
whyNot.3: Stored ATP lasts only seconds and is not the source of lactic acid.

C.q: Which statement about motor units and muscle force is CORRECT?
options: A motor unit is one muscle fiber and all its neurons
A fiber contracts weakly to a weak stimulus
Force increases as more motor units are recruited
Force rises as fewer motor units are recruited
C.why: Whole-muscle force is graded by recruiting more motor units and by increasing stimulation frequency.

whyNot.0: A motor unit is one motor neuron plus all the muscle fibers it supplies.
whyNot.1: Individual fibers respond all-or-none; they do not give partial contractions.
whyNot.3: Recruiting fewer motor units produces less force, not more.

reteach.title: Rowers pulling on a rope
reteach.question: Picture a team of rowers who must grab a rope, pull, let go and reach forward again. How does that match the cross-bridge cycle?

blocks.body: The rope is actin; each rower's hands are a myosin head. A safety cover (tropomyosin) lies over the handholds until calcium, binding troponin, slides it off. Rowers grab (cross-bridge), heave (power stroke), then need a fresh ATP to let go, and splitting ATP re-cocks them to reach forward. The rope slides; the rope itself never gets shorter. No ATP and the rowers cannot let go: rigor mortis.

blocks.text: ATP's surprising job is letting GO. Without it, the rowers stay locked on the rope.

explain.body: Muscle (epimysium) is made of fascicles (perimysium), which are made of fibers, the muscle cells (endomysium). Each fiber contains myofibrils, which are chains of sarcomeres running Z disc to Z disc, built from thin actin and thick myosin filaments.

test.q: Which unit of a myofibril, running from one Z disc to the next, is the contractile unit?
test.why: The sarcomere, from Z disc to Z disc, is the contractile unit of skeletal muscle.

whyNot.0: A fascicle is a bundle of muscle fibers, much larger than a sarcomere.
whyNot.2: Myofilaments (actin and myosin) are the parts inside a sarcomere.
whyNot.3: The sarcolemma is the muscle fiber's cell membrane.

explain.body: ACh from the motor neuron triggers a muscle action potential that travels down the T-tubules. The sarcoplasmic reticulum releases Ca²⁺, which binds troponin. Troponin shifts tropomyosin off actin's myosin-binding sites, so cross-bridges can form.

test.q: What moves tropomyosin off the myosin-binding sites on actin?
test.why: Calcium binds troponin, which changes position and pulls tropomyosin away from the binding sites.

whyNot.0: ATP binding to myosin releases the cross-bridge; it does not move tropomyosin.
whyNot.1: ACh binds receptors on the sarcolemma, not actin.

explain.body: Splitting ATP energizes the myosin head for the power stroke. A new ATP must bind myosin to detach it from actin. Relaxation also needs ATP to pump Ca²⁺ back into the SR. No ATP after death means cross-bridges cannot release: rigor mortis.

test.q: Which pair of roles does ATP play in the cross-bridge cycle?
options: Powers the stroke and releases myosin
Releases ACh and spreads the action potential
test.why: ATP hydrolysis energizes the myosin head, and ATP binding releases myosin from actin.

whyNot.1: Binding troponin and shifting tropomyosin is calcium's role.
whyNot.2: ACh release is a nerve-terminal event, and the action potential is electrical; neither is ATP's cross-bridge job.
whyNot.3: Calcium is stored in the sarcoplasmic reticulum, not by ATP in the sarcolemma.

explain.body: Stored ATP lasts seconds; creatine phosphate about 10–15 s; anaerobic glycolysis is fast but makes lactic acid; aerobic respiration makes the most ATP. Slow-twitch (type I) fibers are oxidative and red, with many mitochondria and myoglobin, for endurance. Fast-twitch (type II) fibers are glycolytic and powerful but tire quickly.

test.q: Which description fits slow-twitch (type I) muscle fibers?
test.why: Slow-twitch fibers are oxidative and red (rich in myoglobin and mitochondria), suited to endurance.

whyNot.0: Glycolytic, powerful and quick to fatigue describes fast-twitch (type II) fibers.
whyNot.1: Slow-twitch fibers have many mitochondria and are built for endurance rather than power.
whyNot.2: Slow-twitch fibers are oxidative, not glycolytic.
